prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map depicts a high-angle egocentric view of a dining area with parallel long red tables and attached benches below the standing camera wearer, where the foreground table surface, cup, salt shaker, and the wearer's left hand on a vertical pole in frame 1 are nearest (roughly 0.4–1.0 m away, within arm's reach), while background tables and standing figures lie 1.5–3.5 m away. Across the 5 frames, the camera wearer pans and turns clockwise toward the right while tilting slightly up: the long table rotates from vertical in frames 1–2 to diagonal in frames 3–5, a person in a black jacket and white cap moves from the right edge (about 1.0–1.5 m away) to sit on the bench directly in front and below the wearer (within 0.7–1.0 m, touching the table edge within arm's reach), and another person in a white shirt enters at the bottom-right foreground of frames 3–4 at ~0.6–0.9 m while a person in a striped shirt stands ~1.5–2.0 m behind them. People are spaced roughly 0.5–1.2 m from one another, with the seated cap wearer facing toward the table and downward away from the camera, the person in dark blue at the upper-left of frame 5 facing toward the table (~1.2 m away), and the standing striped-shirt person turning from facing left in frame 4 to facing away in frame 5. Compared to RGB alone, the depth gradients clearly separate the elevated head/cap of the seated person and the foreground torso of the bottom-right person from the tiled floor and benches 2–3 m behind them despite dark clothing blends. However, the depth map is unreliable along the small cup and shaker on the tabletop (which nearly vanish into the planar table depth in frames 3–5) and suffers from over-saturated bright halos on the white cap in frame 3 and the foreground table corner in frame 2.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates several people and select tabletop/clothing regions across the 5 frames as the camera wearer turns right, tracking the person in the black jacket and white cap moving from the right side of the table (~1.0–1.5 m away in frames 1–2) to sit at the central bench (~0.8–1.0 m in front of and below the wearer in frames 3–5) with their hands on the table edge within arm's reach. It also segments bystanders around the perimeter roughly 0.5–1.5 m apart from each other, including cropped seated figures at the far-left table in frame 1 (~1.5–2.5 m away), the person in the white shirt at the bottom-right foreground of frames 3–4 (~0.6–0.9 m away, within the wearer's arm's reach and facing left toward the table), the standing person in the striped shirt behind them to the upper right (~1.5–2.0 m away), and a person in dark blue seated to the left of the cap wearer in frame 5 (~1.2 m away). Most segmented people are partly occluded by the frame edges or the table—only the arms and legs of the right-side people are visible in frames 1–2, and only the head and shoulders of the bottom-right person appear in frame 3—while the cap wearer faces down toward the tabletop rather than looking at the camera wearer. The segmentation map makes it easier than RGB alone to distinguish overlapping multi-person boundaries in the crowded right-hand aisle of frame 3, where the foreground person, striped-shirt person, and background figures in red and black (~2.0–3.0 m away) stack closely together. However, the map is highly unreliable in class labels and completeness: it misclassifies the red dining table as a 'surfboard' in frames 1 and 5 while completely failing to segment the table, benches, cup, or shaker in frames 2–4, mislabels the cap wearer's scarf as a 'tie' in frame 3, and merges the two people on the right into a single 'person' mask in frame 1.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is almost entirely blank across the 5 frames, detecting zero yellow body skeletons and only three isolated magenta hand skeletons throughout the sequence. In frame 1, it locates the camera wearer's own left hand gripping a vertical post at the bottom-left foreground (~0.4 m away, within immediate arm's reach) and a second person's right hand resting on the upper-right edge of the red table (~1.2 m away, out of the wearer's reach). In frame 2, as the camera turns slightly right, it detects only the right hand of the person in the black jacket touching the right table edge (~1.0 m in front of and to the right of the wearer), and in frame 5 it detects only the face-covering left hand of the person in the dark blue shirt seated across the table (~1.3 m away at the upper-left edge). While these sparse magenta keypoints precisely articulate finger joint orientations and hand contact points on the post, tabletop, and face that are small or motion-blurred in the RGB frames, they provide no information about full-body distances, relative torso positions, or gaze directions. Consequently, the pose map is severely unreliable for scene-level spatial understanding, completely missing all bodies and heads—including the prominent seated person in the white cap 0.8–1.0 m away and the standing people 0.6–2.5 m to the right—and detecting nothing at all in frames 3 and 4 due to the steep downward egocentric viewing angle and severe body truncation at the frame borders.
